name: Zuluk village homestays
price_band: ≈ ₹1,200–1,800 per person a night with all meals (indicative)
summary: Family-run homestays in Zuluk, the old overnight stop for Silk Route mule caravans at about 2,800 m. Simple rooms, thick quilts, home-cooked dal-bhat and momos, and the zigzag road above you at dawn. The usual base for Thambi View Point and Nathang.
body: Zuluk has no hotels. What it has is a row of village houses along the road, most of them with three to six guest rooms on an upper floor, run by the family who lives below. Meals are part of the price: tea on arrival, a simple dinner of rice, dal, a vegetable and often chicken or eggs, then breakfast. Rooms are plain and clean, with heavy blankets rather than heaters in most houses, and hot water by bucket on cold mornings.

We book these homestays for almost every Silk Route trip because they are the right distance from Thambi View Point for sunrise, about 30 to 40 minutes up the loops, and because the families know the road and the weather better than any forecast. Power cuts happen, mobile signal is patchy, and the village goes to bed early. Indian nationals only: a Silk Route permit arranged via Rongli is required. Check current status before you travel.
why: The closest stay to Thambi View Point for a sunrise start
All meals included at a fair village rate
Hosts who read the snow and road conditions every day

faqs.q: Do Zuluk homestays have heaters and hot water?
faqs.a: Some do, many do not. Expect heavy quilts, and hot water by bucket in the morning rather than a running geyser. From November to March night temperatures drop below freezing, so bring thermals, a warm cap and socks for sleeping. If a room heater matters to you, tell us when booking and we will place you in a house that has one, usually for a small extra charge.

faqs.q: Can foreigners stay in Zuluk?
faqs.a: No. Zuluk lies on the restricted Silk Route and the permit issued via Rongli is for Indian nationals only. Foreign travellers cannot stay in Zuluk or drive through it to Nathang. They can see the lower Silk Route villages such as Aritar and Rhenock, which need no special permit beyond the Sikkim entry rules. Rules change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network and ATM in Zuluk?
faqs.a: There is no ATM in Zuluk; the nearest are in Rongli and Rhenock, so carry enough cash for the homestay, tea and tips. Mobile signal is patchy and depends on your operator; BSNL and Jio have worked for most of our guests, but expect dead zones on the loops above the village. Tell family at home you may be out of touch for a night.

name: Nathang Valley homestays
price_band: ≈ ₹1,300–2,000 per person a night with all meals (indicative)
summary: A handful of family homestays in Gnathang, a small high village of yak herders and army neighbours at about 3,750 m. The coldest and highest beds on the Silk Route, best for travellers who are already acclimatised after a night lower down at Zuluk.
body: Gnathang is a cluster of houses, a small gumpa and a temple on a wide valley floor, surrounded by army camps and grazing ground. A few families take guests in rooms heated by a bukhari stove in the kitchen, and serve dinner of rice, dal, potato and whatever meat or eggs came up the road that week. Expect frost on the window inside, even in October.

We only put guests here after a night at Zuluk or Padamchen, never straight from Gangtok, because sleeping at this height without a step on the way is how headaches and breathlessness start. Snow can block the road between December and March. Indian nationals only, with a Silk Route permit arranged via Rongli. Check current status before you travel.
why: Wake up on the open valley floor for clear morning views
Warm family kitchens with a bukhari stove
Puts you close to Kupup and the Nathang war memorial

faqs.q: Is it safe to sleep at Nathang?
faqs.a: For most healthy adults, yes, if you acclimatise first. Sleep one night lower at Zuluk or Padamchen, drink plenty of water, skip alcohol and walk slowly. Headache, nausea or breathlessness at rest are warning signs: tell your driver and go down. Infants, people with heart or lung conditions and anyone who felt unwell at Zuluk should skip Nathang and drive through by day instead.

faqs.q: Are Nathang homestays open in winter?
faqs.a: Some families stay through winter and keep a room or two open, but snow can close the road for days between December and March, and permits are sometimes paused. We confirm with the house the evening before you leave Zuluk. If the road is shut, we keep you at Zuluk and try again next morning. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What toilets do Nathang homestays have?
faqs.a: Most have an attached or shared Western or Indian-style toilet inside the house, but water pipes can freeze on cold nights, so you may get a bucket of warm water instead of a flush. Carry wet wipes and a torch. We choose houses with indoor toilets for families and seniors; ask us if this matters to you.

name: Padamchen village homestays
price_band: ≈ ₹1,200–1,800 per person a night with all meals (indicative)
summary: Quiet forest-edge homestays at Padamchen, about 2,200 m, between Lingtam and Zuluk. A good first night on the Silk Route for families who want to climb gently, with mixed forest of the Pangolakha sanctuary around the village.
body: Padamchen sits below Zuluk on the road up from Rongli, and fewer travellers stop here than at Zuluk, which is exactly why we like it. A few families keep guest rooms in wooden and concrete houses, and cook the usual homestay meals of rice, dal, seasonal greens and chicken, with tea whenever you ask.

Use Padamchen as an acclimatisation step: sleeping here at about 2,200 m before Zuluk and Nathang makes the climb easier on children and older travellers. Evenings are cool even in May; winter nights go below freezing. It lies inside the Silk Route permit area, so Indian nationals only, with the permit arranged via Rongli. Check current status before you travel.
why: A gentler first night before Zuluk and Nathang
Fewer vehicles and a quieter evening than Zuluk
Forest walks on the edge of the Pangolakha sanctuary

faqs.q: Why stay at Padamchen instead of Zuluk?
faqs.a: Padamchen is about 600 m lower than Zuluk, so it is a gentler first night if you are coming straight from the plains or from Gangtok, and it is quieter because most vehicles drive straight through. You lose nothing in the plan: Thambi View Point is around an hour's drive up the road for sunrise, and Zuluk is on the way.

faqs.q: Do we need a permit to stay at Padamchen?
faqs.a: Yes. Padamchen falls inside the restricted Silk Route area, and Indian nationals need the permit arranged via Rongli, usually through a registered agent or your homestay, with a photo ID and passport photos. Foreigners are not allowed beyond the lower villages. Rules and fees change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is food at Padamchen homestays vegetarian-friendly?
faqs.a: Yes. Rice, dal, potato and seasonal vegetables are the base of every homestay meal, and families are used to cooking pure vegetarian food for guests. Tell us ahead if you need no onion and garlic or a Jain meal, as the shop is small and supplies come up from Rongli. Non-vegetarian guests usually get chicken or eggs.

name: Lingtam village homestays
price_band: ≈ ₹1,200–1,700 per person a night with all meals (indicative)
summary: Farmhouse homestays in Lingtam, a warm village at about 1,400 m just above Rongli, where cardamom, maize and vegetables grow around the houses. The lowest and softest start to a Silk Route trip.
body: Lingtam is the first village on the climb from Rongli towards Zuluk, and it still feels like a farming place: terraces of maize and vegetables, cardamom under the trees, cows in the yard. Several families host guests in simple rooms and cook from their own fields when they can.

Because Lingtam is low and mild, it works as a first night for travellers arriving late from Siliguri or Bagdogra, leaving the higher villages for the next day when you are fresh. It sits on the permit side of Rongli, so Indian nationals need the Silk Route permit arranged via Rongli. Check current status before you travel.
why: Mild weather and an easy first night after the plains
Farm food grown around the house
Short drive to Rongli for permits and supplies

faqs.q: How far is Lingtam from Rongli?
faqs.a: About 8–10 km, which takes 30–40 minutes on the climbing road towards Padamchen and Zuluk. Many travellers pick up permits in Rongli in the morning and are at their Lingtam homestay by lunch, or use Lingtam as a late-arrival stop after a long drive from Siliguri. Road works can slow this stretch; check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Lingtam cold?
faqs.a: Not very. At about 1,400 m Lingtam is mild most of the year: shirtsleeves on spring afternoons, a light jacket in the evening, and around 5–10 °C on winter nights. It is the warmest night you will have on the Silk Route, which is why we suggest it for families with young children before going higher.

faqs.q: Can we walk around Lingtam village?
faqs.a: Yes. Lanes run between houses and fields, and your hosts can point you to a short walk to the river or through the cardamom. Ask before photographing people or entering fields, and stay on paths during the monsoon when leeches are out. A walk of an hour or two before dinner is the best way to see village life here.

name: Rolep riverside homestays
price_band: ≈ ₹1,300–2,000 per person a night with all meals (indicative)
summary: Village homestays at Rolep, a farming hamlet at about 1,200 m on the upper Rangpo river, around 20 km beyond Rongli. River sounds, terraced fields and home cooking, for travellers who want a slow night or two away from the Silk Route traffic.
body: Rolep lies upstream of Rongli where the Rangpo river runs down from the high country towards Rorathang and the Teesta. A few families here have opened homestays with rooms looking over the river valley, and they cook what the village grows: rice, maize, squash, greens and local chicken.

Rolep is a place for doing very little: walks along the river, birding in the morning, long meals. It works well before or after the high Silk Route, or as a quiet pair of nights on its own from Gangtok. Roads beyond Rongli can be cut by slides in the monsoon. Ask us whether a permit is needed for your route that season, and check current status before you travel.
why: River-valley quiet with very few other visitors
Home cooking from the family's own fields
A good rest stop before or after the high passes

faqs.q: Where is Rolep and how do we get there?
faqs.a: Rolep is a village on the upper Rangpo river in the Rongli subdivision of Pakyong district, roughly 20 km beyond Rongli bazaar. Most guests come by private car from Gangtok (about 3.5–4 hours) or from Siliguri via Rhenock and Rongli. Shared jeeps run as far as Rongli; from there you need a local taxi, which your homestay can arrange.

faqs.q: Is Rolep good in the monsoon?
faqs.a: It is green and very quiet, but the road beyond Rongli can be blocked by landslides between June and September, and the river runs high and fast. If you come in the rains, keep a spare day and never go down to the water's edge. October to May is the safer and drier window. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What is there to do at Rolep?
faqs.a: Walk the village lanes and the river path, watch birds along the forest edge in the morning, help in the kitchen, and rest. There are no sights to tick off, which is the point. Rolep pairs well with a day trip to Aritar's lake or a night up at Zuluk, and your hosts can suggest longer walks to neighbouring villages.

name: Lungthung homestays
price_band: ≈ ₹1,300–2,000 per person a night with all meals (indicative)
summary: A few high homestays at Lungthung, around 3,800 m, a short drive above Thambi View Point on the road to Nathang. Sunrise over the Kangchenjunga range from the doorstep, for acclimatised travellers who want to skip the dark pre-dawn drive from Zuluk.
body: Lungthung is a scatter of houses and army posts on the open ridge between Thambi View Point and Nathang. A small number of families host guests here in basic rooms warmed by a kitchen stove, and the reason to stay is simple: on a clear morning the Kangchenjunga range lights up in front of you without leaving the house.

This is high and cold, so treat it like Nathang: sleep lower at Zuluk or Padamchen first. Facilities are basic, water may freeze overnight, and snow can close the road from December to March. Indian nationals only, with the Silk Route permit arranged via Rongli. Check current status before you travel.
why: Sunrise on the Kangchenjunga range from the doorstep
No pre-dawn drive up the Zuluk loops
One of the highest family stays on the Silk Route

faqs.q: Lungthung or Zuluk: which is better for sunrise?
faqs.a: Lungthung, if you are acclimatised. You see the sunrise on the Kangchenjunga range from your door instead of driving up the loops in the dark. Zuluk is lower, warmer and easier on the body, and Thambi View Point is 30–40 minutes above it. For families and first-timers we still suggest Zuluk.

faqs.q: How cold is Lungthung at night?
faqs.a: Very cold. Even in October and April night temperatures fall below freezing, and in winter they can drop well below minus 10 °C. Bring a down jacket, thermals, gloves, a warm cap and good socks, and expect a stove in the kitchen rather than heaters in rooms. Pipes can freeze, so water may come in buckets.

faqs.q: Can children stay at Lungthung?
faqs.a: We do not recommend it for babies and young children, who cannot tell you when they feel the altitude. Older children who did well at Zuluk are usually fine for one night. If anyone in your group has a heart or lung condition, sleep at Zuluk and visit Lungthung by day. Ask your doctor before travel if unsure.

name: Aritar lakeside homestays
price_band: ≈ ₹1,500–2,500 per person a night with meals (indicative)
summary: The better family homestays around Lampokhari lake and Aritar bazaar, at about 1,450 m. Rooms with attached baths, good home food and walks to the lake, the gumpa and the 1895 dak bungalow. No special permit needed.
body: Aritar has more homestays than anywhere else on the lower Silk Route, from basic rooms to newer houses with glass-fronted sitting areas facing the hills. We use the better ones within walking distance of Lampokhari lake: attached bathrooms with geysers, clean bedding and families who cook proper Nepali home food, from sel roti at breakfast to gundruk soup at dinner.

Aritar is mild and open to everyone, foreign travellers included, so it is our usual first or last night on any Silk Route trip. Walk round the lake before breakfast, climb to the Aritar Gumpa, or drive up to Mankhim for the views. It is also a fine two-night stop on its own for families who do not want the altitude of Zuluk.
why: Walk to Lampokhari lake and the old dak bungalow
Open to foreign travellers, unlike the upper Silk Route
Attached baths and hot water in the better houses

faqs.q: Do we need a permit for Aritar?
faqs.a: No special permit. Aritar lies below the restricted Silk Route area, so Indian travellers need only the normal Sikkim entry, and foreign travellers need their Sikkim Restricted Area Permit, applied online on the e-FRRO portal. The Silk Route permit via Rongli is only needed for Zuluk, Nathang and the villages above Rongli. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Aritar from Gangtok and Siliguri?
faqs.a: About 67 km from Gangtok, roughly 3 hours by car via Rangpo and Rhenock, and around 110–120 km from Siliguri or NJP, 4–5 hours via Rangpo and Rhenock. NH10 closes after slides in the monsoon, when drivers use the Kalimpong and Pedong road instead. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Is Aritar good for a family with small children?
faqs.a: Yes. At about 1,450 m there is no altitude worry, the lake walk is flat and short, there is boating at Lampokhari, and the homestays are used to children. It is the Silk Route stop we suggest for families who do not want to take toddlers up to Zuluk or Nathang.

name: Mankhim hill homestays
price_band: ≈ ₹1,500–2,500 per person a night with meals (indicative)
summary: Homestays on Mankhim hill above Aritar, near the Kirat Rai temple, at around 1,900–2,000 m. Wide views over the hills to the Kangchenjunga range on clear mornings, with Aritar's lake a short drive below.
body: Mankhim hill rises above Aritar, crowned by the Mangkhim temple of the Kirat Rai community. A few family homestays sit on the slopes near the top, among them the long-running Kanchanjunga Mirror Homestay and The Hill Homestay, and they trade on one thing: the view. On a clear winter morning the Kangchenjunga range stands up across the hills to the north-west.

Rooms are simple to comfortable, meals are home-cooked, and evenings are quieter and cooler than down by the lake. Stay here if you want sunrise from your window and do not mind a short drive or a steep walk to Aritar bazaar. No special permit is needed. Visit the temple respectfully; it is a working place of worship.
why: Sunrise views of the Kangchenjunga range on clear days
Next to the Kirat Rai Mangkhim temple
Cooler and quieter than Aritar bazaar

faqs.q: Can you see Kangchenjunga from Mankhim?
faqs.a: On clear days, yes: the range is visible to the north-west at sunrise, most reliably from October to early March. From April the haze builds and from June to September cloud usually hides it. Even on a cloudy day the view over the Rhenock and Aritar hills is wide. Ask your host for the best spot at dawn.

faqs.q: How far is Mankhim from Aritar lake?
faqs.a: A short drive of 15–20 minutes up a steep road from Aritar, or a stiff walk of about an hour. Most guests drive up for sunrise or for a night, and walk down. If you stay on Mankhim hill, ask your host to arrange a car to the lake and bazaar.

faqs.q: Can visitors enter the Mangkhim temple?
faqs.a: Visitors are generally welcome to see the temple from outside and to walk the grounds, but it is a sacred place of the Kirat Rai community, so dress modestly, ask before taking photographs and follow any instructions from caretakers. During Sakewa celebrations the grounds belong to worshippers; watch from the edges unless invited in.

name: Lampokhari Village Resort
summary: A small village-style resort at Dalapchand, Aritar, close to Lampokhari lake. A step up from homestays, with private rooms, meals on site and parking, for couples and families who want a little more comfort on the lower Silk Route.
body: Lampokhari Village Resort is one of the few stays in Aritar that calls itself a resort rather than a homestay. It sits in Dalapchand, close to the lake, and offers private rooms with attached bathrooms, meals cooked on site and parking for your car, which matters on Aritar's narrow lanes.

We use it for guests who want the comforts of a small hotel in a place that otherwise runs on homestays. It costs more than the lakeside family houses, and you trade some home atmosphere for privacy. Rates rise in October, around Diwali and over Christmas and New Year; book early for those weeks. No special permit is needed for Aritar.
why: Private rooms and on-site meals close to the lake
Parking and easy car access
More comfort than a homestay without leaving Aritar

faqs.q: Is Lampokhari Village Resort near the lake?
faqs.a: Yes, it is in Dalapchand, a short walk or drive from Lampokhari lake and Aritar bazaar. You can walk to the lake for an early circuit before breakfast and be back for tea. Ask for a room facing the valley when booking.

faqs.q: Does the resort serve meals?
faqs.a: Yes. Meals are cooked on site and usually include breakfast and dinner on a meal plan, with lunch on request. Food is a mix of Indian and simple Nepali dishes. There are a few small eateries in Aritar bazaar if you want a change.

faqs.q: Should we choose the resort or a homestay in Aritar?
faqs.a: Choose the resort if you want privacy, a car park and a more hotel-like room. Choose one of the better lakeside homestays if you want home food, family company and a lower bill. Both are good bases for the lake, the gumpa and Mankhim. We can price both for your dates.

name: Vivanta Sikkim, Pakyong
summary: IHCL's Vivanta hotel at Pakyong, set among paddy terraces and bamboo a short drive from Pakyong airport. A heated outdoor pool, a Jiva spa and valley views: the most comfortable stay in the district and a calm alternative to staying in Gangtok.
body: Vivanta Sikkim was the Indian Hotels Company's first hotel in Sikkim, built on the slopes near Pakyong among paddy fields and bamboo, about 7–8 km from the airport and roughly an hour from Gangtok. It has a temperature-controlled outdoor pool with mountain views, a Jiva spa, an all-day restaurant serving Sikkimese dishes alongside a wider menu, and a bar.

We suggest it for couples and families who want hotel comfort at the start or end of a Silk Route trip, or who prefer a quiet country base to Gangtok's traffic. Pakyong airport has no scheduled flights at present, so plan to arrive via Bagdogra (about 4 hours) or NJP. Check current status before you travel.
why: Heated outdoor pool and spa, rare in East Sikkim
Quiet rural setting about an hour from Gangtok
A comfortable start or end to the Silk Route

faqs.q: Can we fly into Pakyong to stay at Vivanta?
faqs.a: Not at present. Pakyong airport opened in 2018 but has no scheduled commercial flights now. Fly to Bagdogra (IXB) and drive about 4–4.5 hours via Rangpo, or take a train to NJP. Your driver can reach Vivanta without going through Gangtok. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Vivanta Pakyong from Gangtok?
faqs.a: About 30–35 km, roughly 1 to 1.5 hours by car via Ranipool, depending on traffic. That makes day trips to Gangtok, Rumtek and the Ranipool area easy, and Aritar is about 1.5–2 hours away via Rorathang and Rhenock.

faqs.q: Is Vivanta Sikkim a good base for the Silk Route?
faqs.a: It is a good first or last night. From Pakyong it is around 2 hours to Rongli for the Silk Route permit and the climb to Zuluk. We would not stay here every night of a Silk Route trip, as the drives to Zuluk and Nathang are long; sleep in the village homestays up the road instead.
